query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7, the stability of the initial high-temperature BCC phase is governed by a competition between high-temperature entropy stabilization and a thermodynamic driving force for local chemical ordering induced by Al. At high temperatures, configurational entropy sustains a homogeneous BCC structure, but as the alloy is cooled slowly or annealed, the reduced entropy allows Al to promote local ordering that destabilizes the BCC phase.
generation.material_initial_state: Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy in a high-temperature BCC disordered state
generation.intervention: Subject samples to controlled thermal histories—specifically, comparing rapid quenching (to preserve high-temperature entropy) versus slow cooling or prolonged annealing (to enable Al-driven local ordering)
generation.conditions: Use identical compositions and initial conditions while varying only the thermal treatment. Temperature regimes should span from well above the BCC stability limit to below the anticipated onset of ordering. Atmosphere and sample dimensions should be controlled to minimize extrinsic effects.
generation.structural_mediator: Local chemical ordering around Al atoms (and the resulting short-range clustering of other elements) that may lead to the emergence of secondary phases
generation.mechanism: At elevated temperatures, the alloy exists as a random BCC solid solution stabilized chiefly by high configurational entropy. Upon slow cooling, the reduction in entropy and increased impact of Al’s chemical affinity promote local ordering. This ordering reduces the free energy locally enough to trigger phase transformation, whereas rapid quenching freezes in the high-entropy disordered BCC state.
generation.predicted_outcome: Rapidly quenched samples will retain a homogeneous BCC phase, while slowly cooled or annealed samples will exhibit evidence of local chemical ordering (e.g., composition fluctuations or incipient secondary phases) indicative of the destabilization of the BCC phase.
generation.baseline: The high-temperature BCC state achieved by rapid quenching, which minimizes the opportunity for Al-induced ordering
generation.boundary: The hypothesis applies within the temperature window where the entropy contribution and the ordering driving force are competitive; at temperatures significantly above this window, entropy dominates, and at much lower temperatures, kinetic limitations may prevent full equilibrium phase transformations.
generation.uncertainty: The quantitative extent of local ordering and the precise thermal conditions at which the ordering becomes sufficient to destabilize the BCC phase are uncertain and may vary with minute changes in processing parameters.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 samples under identical conditions. One set is rapidly quenched from a temperature well above the BCC stability limit, and the other set is subjected to slow cooling or held at an intermediate annealing temperature near the expected ordering transition. Characterize both sets for phase distribution and chemical ordering.
measurements: X-ray diffraction (XRD) for phase identification and lattice parameter shifts
Transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to detect nano-scale ordering or secondary phases
Atom probe tomography (APT) for evaluating local chemical ordering around Al atoms
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the slowly cooled or annealed samples show no statistically significant difference in local ordering or phase separation (as compared to the rapidly quenched baseline) under conditions where such ordering is thermodynamically expected, then the hypothesis that Al-induced local ordering governs the phase stability of the BCC phase is falsified.

Evaluation of Equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu System and Subsequent Derivation of a Non-Equiatomic MnFeCoNiCu Alloy

Abstract: AbstractInvestigation into non-equiatomic high-entropy alloys has grown in recent years due to questions about the role of entropy stabilization in forming single-phase solid solutions. Non-equiatomic alloys have been shown to retain the outstanding mechanical properties exhibited by their equiatomic counterparts and even improve electrical, thermal, and magnetic properties, albeit with relaxed composition bounds. However, much remains to understand the processing–structure–property relationships in all classes of so-called high-entropy alloys (HEAs). Here, we are motivated by the natural phenomena of crystal growth and equilibrium conditions to introduce a method of HEA development where controlled processing conditions determine the most probable and stable composition. This is demonstrated by cooling an equiatomic CrMnFeCoNiCu alloy from the melt steadily over 3 days (cooling rate ~4 °C/h). The result is an alloy containing large Cr-rich precipitates and an almost Cr-free matrix exhibiting compositions within the MnFeCoNiCu system (with trace amounts of Cr). Fro

Entropy-stabilized oxides

Abstract: Configurational disorder can be compositionally engineered into mixed oxide by populating a single sublattice with many distinct cations. The formulations promote novel and entropy-stabilized forms of crystalline matter where metal cations are incorporated in new ways. Here, through rigorous experiments, a simple thermodynamic model, and a five-component oxide formulation, we demonstrate beyond reasonable doubt that entropy predominates the thermodynamic landscape, and drives a reversible solid-state transformation between a multiphase and single-phase state. In the latter, cation distributions are proven to be random and homogeneous. The findings validate the hypothesis that deliberate configurational disorder provides an orthogonal strategy to imagine and discover new phases of crystalline matter and untapped opportunities for property engineering. The composition of oxide compounds controls many of their properties and electronic phases. Here, the authors show that entropy and configurational disorder can stabilize new phases of oxides, potentially enabling a better engineering of their properties.

On the evolving nature of c/a ratio in a hexagonal close-packed epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys

Abstract: Activation of different slip systems in hexagonal close packed (h.c.p.) metals depends primarily on the c/a ratio, which is an intrinsic property that can be altered through alloying addition. In conventional h.c.p. alloys where there is no diffusion-less phase transformation and associated transformation volume change with deformation, the c/a ratio remains constant during deformation. In the present study, c/a ratio and transformation volume change of h.c.p. epsilon martensite phase in transformative high entropy alloys (HEAs) were quantified as functions of alloy chemistry, friction stir processing and tensile deformation. The study revealed that while intrinsic c/a is dependent on alloying elements, c/a of epsilon in transformative HEAs changes with processing and deformation. This is attributed to transformation volume change induced dependence of h.c.p. lattice parameters on microstructure and stress state. Lower than ideal c/a ratio promotes non-basal pyramidal 〈c + a〉 slip and deformation twinning in epsilon phase of transformative HEAs.
